passage: In the university hostel, Wasim had loved rooming with Thomas at first. Thomas called him "the smartest guy on the floor" and dragged him to every party. By second term it was different. When Wasim got a B, Thomas laughed: "Guess I'm the brains now." When Thomas lost the room key, it was Wasim's fault. When Wasim talked about his grandfather being unwell, Thomas turned the talk to his own football trial. Wasim started double-checking everything he said. One evening the hostel warden, Mr Pinto, found him sitting on the stairs. "You've gone very quiet this term." Wasim hesitated, then told him. Mr Pinto listened. "None of that sounds like your fault. Let's talk about a room change, and keep talking."

qa.q: What did Thomas call Wasim at first?
qa.a: He called him "the smartest guy on the floor".

qa.q: How did Wasim feel by second term, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt small and unsure of himself; he started double-checking everything he said.

qa.q: What turning point came on the stairs?
qa.a: Wasim told the warden what was happening, and Mr Pinto said it wasn't his fault and offered to talk about a room change, giving him an outside view.

qa.q: How might Mr Pinto see Wasim's quietness this term?
qa.a: He saw it as a sign something was wrong, which is why he checked in gently.

grounding: A student flattered early by a self-centred roommate grows small and blamed, and recognises the pattern with a trusted warden.

subtype: Friend or partner on the receiving end [Receiver]
passage:
Dear Rashmi-di,
You're the only one I can say this to. When I met Kunal in first year, he told everyone I was the cleverest girl in college. I felt like I was glowing. Now, a year later, I don't recognise myself. If I talk about my day, he talks over me. When he forgot my birthday, somehow I ended up apologising for "making it a big deal". Last week I cried after he called my painting "cute for a beginner", and he said I was too sensitive. I've started believing him. Maybe I am. Is it me?
Can I come home this weekend and talk properly? I think I need someone outside all this to tell me what they see.
Love,
Trisha

qa.q: What did Kunal call Trisha's painting?
qa.a: He called it "cute for a beginner".

qa.q: What is Trisha doubting now, and why?
qa.a: She doubts herself, wondering if she is too sensitive, because Kunal keeps blaming her and she has started believing him.

qa.q: What choice does Trisha make in this letter, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She reaches out to Rashmi-di, a trusted outsider, to talk properly, which can help her see the pattern clearly.

qa.q: How might Rashmi feel reading "Is it me?"
qa.a: She may feel worried and protective, and keen to reassure Trisha and help her see what is happening.

grounding: A young woman flattered early by a partner now feels small, blamed and unheard, and turns to a trusted cousin to see the pattern.

passage: When Samir first came to Noor's house in Aligarh with his parents, he praised everything: her poetry, her cooking, her English. For weeks after the engagement he called every night. Now, three months on, the calls were all about him: his promotion, his plans, his cricket team. When she mentioned her college poetry prize, he said, "Small-town competitions," and changed the subject. When he missed her mother's birthday, somehow it was her fault for not reminding him. Noor began wondering if she really was boring. One afternoon her Khala found her tearing up a poem. Noor told her everything. Khala listened, then said quietly, "Beti, you're not the problem. Let's talk about this with your Ammi tonight."

qa.q: How was Noor feeling about herself three months after the engagement?

qa.a: A trusted outsider could name the pattern and help Noor see she was not the problem, and involve her Ammi that night.

qa.a: Khala sees that Noor is being blamed and belittled, and says clearly that Noor is not the problem.

subtype: Friend or partner on the receiving end [Receiver]
passage: When Mei met Santiago at the language exchange in Barcelona, he told her she was the most interesting person in the room. For two months she floated. By spring something had shifted. He talked about his band for an hour and yawned when she mentioned her thesis. If she was hurt, he said she was "too dramatic". If he was late, she had "confused the time". Mei began rehearsing sentences before saying them and wondering if she was the problem. In April she mentioned it, almost as a joke, to her thesis adviser, Dr Ruiz. Dr Ruiz put down her pen. "You used to argue with me every week, Mei. Now you apologise for everything. Would you talk to the student counselling service? I'll walk you down."

qa.q: What did Santiago talk about for an hour?
qa.a: His band.

qa.q: What was Mei feeling by spring?
qa.a: She felt small, unheard and full of self-doubt, rehearsing sentences and wondering if she was the problem.

qa.q: Why was Dr Ruiz's response helpful?
qa.a: Dr Ruiz noticed a real change in Mei, named it and offered to walk her to counselling that day.

qa.q: How does Dr Ruiz see the change in Mei?
qa.a: Dr Ruiz sees that Mei has gone from arguing confidently to apologising for everything, which is worrying.

grounding: Shows a young adult who is flattered early, then blamed and unheard, and a trusted outsider noticing the change.

subtype: Friend or partner on the receiving end [Receiver]
passage:
In the college counselling centre, Harish twisted his hands in his lap. "At first Rashmi said I was the smartest person she'd ever met. She'd tell everyone."
The counsellor nodded. "And now?"
"Now if I talk about my day, she changes the subject to hers. If she's late, it's my fault for 'rushing' her. Last week I got a good grade and she said, 'Must've been an easy test.'" He laughed, but it came out thin. "Maybe I'm too sensitive. Maybe I really am the problem."
"You've said 'maybe I'm the problem' three times today," the counsellor said gently. "What was it like before you met her?"
Harish was quiet. "I was sure of myself. I had friends I saw every week."
"Let's look at that together, over the next few sessions. And I'd like you to reconnect with one of those friends this week."
Harish nodded slowly.

qa.q: What did Rashmi say when Harish got a good grade?
qa.a: "Must've been an easy test."

qa.q: How does Harish feel about himself now?
qa.a: He feels small and full of self-doubt, wondering if he is too sensitive or really the problem.

qa.q: Why is talking with the counsellor an important step for Harish?
qa.a: A trusted outsider can help him see the pattern of being flattered, then blamed and unheard, before it wears down his confidence further.

qa.q: How does the counsellor see Harish's repeated "maybe I'm the problem"?
qa.a: The counsellor notices it as a sign of rising self-doubt and gently turns him toward how sure of himself he used to be.

grounding: Shows a young adult flattered early then made to feel small and blamed by a self-centred partner, recognising the pattern with a counsellor.
